phonemes.articulation: Close both lips and maintain voicing into the release.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast unvoiced /p/.

phonemes.title: Voiced dental stop
phonemes.articulation: Place the tongue near the upper teeth and release with voicing.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast /t/.

phonemes.title: Close-mid e
phonemes.articulation: Raise the front of the tongue moderately and keep the lips unrounded.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast /ɛ/, which is more open.

phonemes.title: Unvoiced lip-to-teeth fricative
phonemes.articulation: Touch the lower lip lightly to the upper teeth and let air pass.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast voiced /v/.

phonemes.title: Close front i
phonemes.articulation: Raise the front of the tongue with unrounded lips.
phonemes.contrast: Keep it steady rather than turning it into a diphthong.

phonemes.title: Palatal glide
phonemes.articulation: Move quickly through a tongue position close to /i/ without making a full extra syllable.
phonemes.contrast: Written ill does not always represent /j/: ville is an exception.

phonemes.title: Unvoiced back stop
phonemes.articulation: Close the back of the tongue against the soft palate and release.
phonemes.contrast: C before e or i often represents /s/ instead.

phonemes.title: Lateral l
phonemes.articulation: Touch the tongue near the upper teeth and let air pass around its sides.
phonemes.contrast: Avoid an added vowel between consonants.

phonemes.title: Lip nasal
phonemes.articulation: Close both lips and allow air to pass through the nose.
phonemes.contrast: A nasal consonant differs from a nasal vowel.

phonemes.title: Front nasal
phonemes.articulation: Place the tongue near the upper teeth and let air pass through the nose.
phonemes.contrast: Do not add /n/ after a nasal vowel unless the word calls for it.

phonemes.title: Close-mid o
phonemes.articulation: Keep the tongue toward the back with a relatively closed rounded vowel.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast the more open /ɔ/ in porte.

phonemes.title: Unvoiced lip stop
phonemes.articulation: Close both lips, then release without a strong English-style puff of air.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast voiced /b/.

phonemes.title: Unvoiced s
phonemes.articulation: Let air pass along the tongue near the upper teeth without voicing.
phonemes.contrast: A single written s between vowels often sounds /z/.

phonemes.title: Unvoiced dental stop
phonemes.articulation: Place the tongue near the upper teeth and release with little aspiration.
phonemes.contrast: Some regional varieties affricate t before certain vowels.

phonemes.title: Close back rounded ou
phonemes.articulation: Raise the back of the tongue and round the lips.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast tu /ty/.

phonemes.title: Voiced lip-to-teeth fricative
phonemes.articulation: Use the /f/ position with vocal-fold vibration.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast /f/.

phonemes.title: Rounded back glide
phonemes.articulation: Move quickly from a rounded back position toward the following vowel.
phonemes.contrast: Oi commonly represents /wa/.

phonemes.title: Close front rounded u
phonemes.articulation: Start from tongue position /i/ and round the lips without moving the tongue backward.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast tout /tu/.

phonemes.title: Voiced z
phonemes.articulation: Use the /s/ position with voicing.
phonemes.contrast: A plural liaison often introduces /z/.

phonemes.title: Close-mid rounded eu
phonemes.articulation: Use a front mid vowel with rounded lips.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast the more open /œ/ in sœur.

phonemes.title: Back nasal
phonemes.articulation: Close the back of the tongue against the soft palate while allowing nasal airflow.
phonemes.contrast: This sound occurs especially in borrowed words.

phonemes.title: Open-mid rounded eu
phonemes.articulation: Keep the tongue toward the front, lower than for /ø/, and round the lips.
phonemes.contrast: Do not replace this sound with English er.

phonemes.title: Nasal un
phonemes.articulation: Use a rounded nasal front vowel where the accent retains this distinction.
phonemes.contrast: Many French speakers merge /œ̃/ with /ɛ̃/; regional models differ.

phonemes.title: Back a
phonemes.articulation: Keep the tongue low and farther back than /a/. This distinction varies by region.
phonemes.contrast: Compare patte /pat/ in accents retaining the distinction.

phonemes.title: Nasal an/en
phonemes.articulation: Produce a low back vowel while allowing air through the nose; do not add a separate final n.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast the oral vowel plus consonant in a word such as année.

phonemes.title: Open-mid o
phonemes.articulation: Open the jaw more than for /o/ and retain rounded lips.
phonemes.contrast: The /o/–/ɔ/ distribution varies across accents.

phonemes.title: Nasal on
phonemes.articulation: Round the lips and allow nasal airflow while keeping one vowel sound.
phonemes.contrast: Compare bon /bɔ̃/ and bonne /bɔn/.

phonemes.title: Schwa
phonemes.articulation: Use a short central vowel. Its presence varies with rhythm, region and surrounding consonants.
phonemes.contrast: Schwa deletion is contextual, not a rule to delete every written e.

phonemes.title: Open-mid e
phonemes.articulation: Lower the tongue more than for /e/ while keeping the lips unrounded.
phonemes.contrast: Compare été /ete/ and mère /mɛʁ/.

phonemes.title: Nasal in/ain
phonemes.articulation: Produce an open front nasal vowel without appending an English n.
phonemes.contrast: Spellings in, ain, ein and others can represent this vowel.

phonemes.title: Voiced back stop
phonemes.articulation: Close the back of the tongue against the soft palate and release with voicing.
phonemes.contrast: G before e or i often represents /ʒ/ instead.

phonemes.title: Rounded front glide
phonemes.articulation: Keep a front tongue position like /y/ and glide rapidly to the following vowel.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast the back glide /w/.

phonemes.title: Gn nasal
phonemes.articulation: Raise the middle of the tongue toward the hard palate while allowing nasal airflow.
phonemes.contrast: Some speakers use a sequence close to /nj/.

phonemes.title: French r
phonemes.articulation: Produce a voiced or partly devoiced uvular friction sound toward the back of the mouth; regional r sounds vary.
phonemes.contrast: Do not force excessive throat tension.

phonemes.title: Ch sound
phonemes.articulation: Round the lips slightly and direct air behind the alveolar ridge without voicing.
phonemes.contrast: Contrast /ʒ/ in jour.

phonemes.title: Voiced ch-like sound
phonemes.articulation: Use the /ʃ/ position with voicing.
phonemes.contrast: Written j and soft g often represent this sound.

pronunciation_rules.title: U and ou contrast
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Keep the tongue forward for /y/ and back for /u/; both use rounded lips.

pronunciation_rules.title: Silent final letters
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Final written consonants are often silent, but lexical exceptions and inflections matter. Compare the dictionary forms.

pronunciation_rules.title: Determiner liaison
pronunciation_rules.explanation: An otherwise silent final consonant is pronounced in common determiner + vowel-initial noun groups. The sound can differ from the spelling.

pronunciation_rules.title: Nasal versus oral vowel
pronunciation_rules.explanation: A nasal vowel is not a vowel followed by a separate n. Doubling a nasal consonant can change the vowel to oral.

pronunciation_rules.title: Elision before a vowel
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Words such as je, ne, le and la can lose their vowel before a vowel or mute h. Write the required apostrophe.

pronunciation_rules.title: Subject-pronoun liaison
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Liaison is expected between a subject pronoun and a following vowel-initial verb.

pronunciation_rules.title: No liaison after et
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Do not insert a t sound after the conjunction et.

pronunciation_rules.title: Aspirated h blocks linking
pronunciation_rules.explanation: An aspirated h is normally silent but blocks elision and liaison. Check the dictionary: the written h alone does not identify the class.

pronunciation_rules.title: Mute h permits elision
pronunciation_rules.explanation: A mute h permits the same elision and liaison as a vowel-initial word.

pronunciation_rules.title: Enchaînement
pronunciation_rules.explanation: An already pronounced final consonant can join the following vowel; this is not the creation of a new liaison consonant.

pronunciation_rules.title: Rhythm and prominence
pronunciation_rules.explanation: French prominence generally falls near the end of a rhythmic group, not strongly on every individual word. Practise the phrase as a group.

pronunciation_rules.title: Variable schwa
pronunciation_rules.explanation: The presence of /ə/ depends on rhythm, region and neighbouring consonants. Learn a careful model before practising reductions.

pronunciation_rules.title: Plus changes with context
pronunciation_rules.explanation: Plus can be /ply/, /plys/ or /plyz/ depending on meaning, position and liaison. Do not apply one citation form everywhere.
